question: A 61-year-old man comes to the physician because of a 6-month history of epigastric pain and a 9-kg (20-lb) weight loss. He feels full and bloated even after eating small portions of food. His hemoglobin concentration is 9.5 g/dL with a mean corpuscular volume of 78 μm3. Test of the stool for occult blood is positive. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy shows a 2-cm raised lesion with central ulceration on the lesser curvature of the stomach. Histologic examination of a gastric biopsy specimen from the lesion is most likely to show which of the following?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Chronic epigastric pain and weight loss -> suspicion of gastrointestinal malignancy -> further investigations needed -> 80% confidence. CHAIN: Positive stool occult blood test -> concern for gastrointestinal bleeding -> possible malignancy -> 70% confidence. CHAIN: Raised lesion with central ulceration on lesser curvature of the stomach -> likely gastric malignancy -> 90% confidence. CHAIN: Histologic examination of gastric biopsy from the lesion -> expected to show neoplastic changes -> 95% confidence. CHAIN: Neoplastic changes in gastric biopsy -> possible findings of gland-forming cuboidal cells -> 80% confidence. CHAIN: Neoplastic changes in gastric biopsy -> unlikely to show lymphocytic aggregates with noncaseating granulomas -> 80%
analysis: The clinical presentation of epigastric pain, weight loss, feeling full, and bloated along with the findings of low hemoglobin, positive stool occult blood, and a raised lesion with central ulceration on endoscopy are suggestive of gastric cancer. The histologic examination of a gastric biopsy specimen from the lesion in gastric cancer typically shows gland-forming cuboidal cells.
